cells.tense: The hours you keep are landing, and you can feel them landing in how you sit with people now.
cells.ask: Offer one more shared hour than feels needed, and let what it clears do the clearing.
cells.core:
The work you do alone is coming back to you as steadiness around other people. You sit down with someone and you're actually there — not rehearsing what you'll say, not measuring yourself against them. That steadiness was built in quiet hours nobody watched, and it's the reason your attention holds when someone else's is shaky.

Something that was only getting in the way can drop now, and it drops on its own when you see it clearly — an old rule about who to be in this room, a way of bracing you picked up without noticing. Dismantling it by force isn't required. Let one more hour of the work be shared instead of private, and watch how much lighter the room gets.
cells.sheetLine: The practice you keep alone is showing up as steadiness with people.
cells.verb: keeping a small steady practice lit by attention
cells.place: where you meet another and stand alongside them

cells.tense: You're braced for the day the practice falls apart, and you're spending the present keeping that day from arriving.
cells.ask: Let one practice end on purpose, and see what's still standing when you do.
cells.core:
When this is working, the work has edges — you put it down, you pick a person up, and the two aren't at war. Those edges are gone. You keep refining past the point where refining did anything, and you tell yourself the solitude is chosen when it's closer to a door you've stopped letting anyone through. The fear underneath is that if you stop, you'll find out the whole thing was held together by your grip.

Finishing is its own thing, and it isn't the same as quitting. Close one piece of the practice because it's done, not because it failed, and let the hours it frees go toward someone. The grip is what's costing you; the work survives without it.

cells.tense: The practice went quiet a while back, and you've been standing at the edge of it since.
cells.ask: Start back tiny and even — ten honest minutes given the same weight as ten minutes given to someone else.
cells.core:
When it's going well, the practice has a modest place. You give it a corner of the day the way you'd give a friend a chair, no more, no less, and it feeds the hours you spend with people instead of eating them. The doing is steady and unremarkable, and it holds you up without asking anything dramatic of you.

What's missing isn't willpower — it's the ordinary sense that your own time counts the same as anyone else's. So keep the return to the practice small, and keep it even. A quarter hour for the work, fairly measured against what you'd give away without blinking. The steadiness comes back through that fairness, not through pushing at what went quiet.
cells.sheetLine: The practice doesn't need more effort. It needs its hours counted as fairly as anyone else's.

cells.tense: You're already at the practice — hours deep, most weeks — and you'd describe almost none of it that way.
cells.ask: Name one thing you do on purpose and have been calling it just how you are.
cells.core:
Some of what you've gotten good at came from showing up over and over, and that's the part you keep leaving out of the story. The skill is real and it's folded into how you're with people — the patience you bring, the way you can stay in a hard conversation. You frame it as though it arrived by itself, and when you call it refusal instead of repetition, you're doing the same thing with a harder word.

What you're moving through won't come with the whole road visible. Nobody gets that, and you don't need it. One clear step in front of you is enough to take, and it usually comes as a picture of the next thing rather than a plan. Say aloud that one thing you've been doing deliberately, and let the saying settle it as yours.
